title: Course introduction
lead: Database systems: motivation, definitions, data abstraction and the scope of the Edinburgh course.
goals: Abstraction, data models and course scope

sections.title: Motivation for database systems
sections.html:
Purpose and motivation

The course asks why database systems are necessary, what their internals do and how their components fit together. Applications generate persistent facts and need queries and updates over them. Cheaper data generation and cheaper processing increase the scale of this problem; knowing a file format is insufficient for managing it.

The three motivations are practical usefulness, the central role of data in society, and the role of scalable data management throughout computing.

PDF pp. 1–4

Scale, filtering and the capacity gap

The Domo chart describes data generated per minute in its 2023 edition. The CERN example contrasts raw detector output with successive reductions before storage: the displayed rates fall from 600,000,000 GB/s to 25 GB/s and then 1050 MB/s. These are source-specific historical illustrations, not current hardware specifications.

The systems implication is that collection, selection, transfer, storage and processing capacity must be designed together. Not every generated byte can be treated as equally valuable or immediately processable.

PDF pp. 5–9

sections.title: Database, DBMS and file-based storage
sections.html:
Database and DBMS

A database is related data organised to represent a domain. A DBMS is software mediating users’ access to that data. A banking application and the stored account facts are different from the software enforcing and executing their operations.

The university scenario includes students, instructors and courses. Operations add those entities, register students, produce class lists, record grades and compute transcripts. The same stored facts support several applications; the DBMS should provide a consistent interface rather than requiring each application to manage its own files.

PDF pp. 10–12

The source CSV query

The source Instructor relation contains (Jones, CS, 95000), (Smith, Physics, 75000) and (Gold, CS, 62000). Finding CS instructors returns Jones and Gold. With CSV, application code must read lines, parse fields and compare the department field before producing names.

Changing column positions or encoding changes that parsing code. This is the coupling the DBMS interface removes: the application names logical attributes while the system manages their physical representation.

PDF pp. 13–14

File-management limitations

  • Redundancy duplicates facts and makes a change such as CS → Computer Science require several coordinated edits.
  • Each new question needs new parsing/search code; without an index, key lookup scans the file.
  • A failed multi-write update can leave a partial result, requiring transaction atomicity.
  • Integrity constraints must be enforced across every write path.
  • Concurrent writers need coordination; permissions must distinguish who can read or modify each part.
  • Other programs need an API rather than knowledge of private file layouts.

PDF pp. 15–17

sections.title: Abstraction, data models and course scope
sections.html:
Abstraction and data models

The physical level specifies record bytes and storage structures. The logical level specifies relations and attributes. Views expose selected logical information and can hide salary data. Physical data independence allows storage changes without rewriting logical queries; logical independence limits the effect of logical-schema changes on views and applications.

A data model is a vocabulary for describing data; a schema is one description using it; an instance is its current data. The source lists relational, key-value, graph, document, array, hierarchical and network models. Its popularity chart measures mentions and related signals, not execution performance.

PDF pp. 18–20

Technical scope and prerequisites

The course connects principles (independence, declarative queries, isolation, consistency), algorithms (search, optimisation, execution, concurrency) and system composition. Disk-oriented DBMS internals lead from storage/files through indexes and query processing to transactions and distributed/parallel execution.

Required background includes introductory relational databases, query languages, sorting/searching, asymptotic analysis, basic P/NP complexity and programming. The Java assignment belongs to the Edinburgh course context; its language choice does not change the algorithms being taught.

PDF pp. 21–24

sections.title: Edinburgh course organisation and references
sections.html:
Teaching, assessment and source context

The introductory deck names Milos Nikolic for systems and Andreas Pieris for query theory. It describes live/recorded lectures in weeks 1–10, online quizzes, revision classes in weeks 3/5/7/9 and no official practical labs. The website’s labs are therefore supplementary.

Edinburgh’s stated assessment is 50% a Java DBMS programming assignment and 50% an in-person exam. The source records release in week 2, a 19 March noon deadline, 6–8 mandatory exam questions and one double-sided A4 notes sheet. These are historical Edinburgh arrangements, not local course deadlines or permission rules.

The systems textbook is Ramakrishnan/Gehrke; the theory text is linked from the schedule. Assignment work must be individual under the source’s misconduct rules; Piazza is the stated communication channel. The final slide credits the teaching material’s contributors.

PDF pp. 25–36

quiz.question: Changing a record’s byte position primarily belongs to which level?
quiz.explanation: A byte position is a physical representation detail; the schema describes the meaning and structure of the data.
